approved: Textile, Clothing and Footwear Investment and Innovation Programs Amendment Bill 2014

Tony Zappia This bill amends the Textile, Clothing and Footwear Investment and Innovation Programs Act 1999. The purpose of the bill is to close the Clothing and Household Textile (Building Innovative Capability) Scheme, otherwise known as the BIC scheme, and the Textile, Clothing and Footwear Small Business Program on 30 June 2014. That is one year ahead of the original time intended for closure of those two programs. The closing of the programs one year early would provide some $25 million of savings to this government but at a detrimental cost to our TCF industries—our textile, clothing and footwear industries. It is just another example of this government turning its back on the manufacturing sector in Australia. I note from the second reading speech of the parliamentary secretary that he provided no justification or explanation whatsoever as to why the two programs were being terminated a year earlier than intended. The BIC scheme is a $22.5 million program that supports innovation and development of sustainable and internationally competitive manufacturing and design industries for clothing and household textiles in Australia. Payments for BIC grants are retrospective. They are based on investment decisions firms have already made to improve their operations. The final program eligibility year is 2014-15, with final payments to be made in 2015-16—that was the intent. Grants are available for research and development, including innovative product design activities, innovative process improvements, market research and some industrial property rights. The TCF Small Business Program provides grants of up to $50,000 for projects to improve the business enterprise culture of TCF businesses. Funding of $2.5 million is available per year over a 10-year program period which commenced in 2006-07. Introduced a bill closing the textile, clothing and footwear industry's BIC Scheme and Small Business Program a year earlier than planned, reducing combined grant funding by $25 million, noting the clothing tariff will fall from 10 per cent to five per cent from 1 January 2015.

Defended closing the TCF grants a year early to save $25 million, noting the industry now employs about 40,000 people, and highlighted the new free trade agreement with Korea, expected to create at least 15,000 jobs and add $650 million annually to the economy.

Opposed the early closure of the BIC scheme, warning it would undermine business trust in government, and said Bruck Textiles in Wangaratta, which employs over 200 people, relies on an expected $500,000 to $700,000 grant supporting 15 to 17 research jobs.

Supported closing the TCF grant programs, recalling import duties on fabric of around 35 per cent when he worked in the industry in the 1980s, now falling to 5 per cent from January 2015, and urged the ACCC to block any merger between David Jones and Myer as anti-competitive for fashion designers.

Supported ending what he called 'corporate welfare' for the textile industry, saying tariffs would fall from 10 to 5 per cent from January 2015, and argued free trade remains the only sustainable economic path, a principle set out in Adam Smith's 1776 Wealth of Nations.

Summed up the TCF bill, correcting claims by opposition members, and noted the Commonwealth has provided more than $1.2 billion in TCF grants since 2001-02, arguing tough budget decisions were needed to address $667 billion in inherited debt.
